title: It Still Feels Like Summer in Parts of the US. Blame El Niño
gist: The US just had its hottest summer on record with heat persisting deep into September, driven by a record-setting El Niño layered on top of climate-change-raised baseline temperatures, and forecasters expect above-normal warmth to continue through fall and winter.

insights.claim: The US just experienced its hottest summer in recorded history in 2026, with tens of thousands of heat records broken nationwide during the year.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: A record hot US summer directly raises cooling-degree-day demand, relevant to utility earnings, natural gas/power demand forecasts, and grid-stress risk into peak season.
insights.quote: the hottest summer in US history
insights.locator: The blast of unseasonably warm air

insights.claim: Roughly 44,000 record daytime highs and more than 53,000 record-high overnight minimum temperatures were recorded at US weather stations in 2026, versus only about 21,500 record lows — a ratio of roughly four heat records for every one cold record.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: The ~4:1 heat-to-cold record ratio is a concrete, citable metric for quantifying the pace of warming versus prior years — useful as a recurring benchmark to track quarter over quarter.
insights.quote: only about 21,500 low-temperature records fell, or around one cold record for every four heat records
insights.locator: That includes nearly 44,000 record daytime highs

insights.claim: Salt Lake City hit 109°F on July 12, 2026, its hottest temperature ever recorded since record-keeping began in 1874, and Washington, DC tied its all-time warmest overnight low of 84°F on July 3, with records dating to 1871.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: Century-plus-old records falling in specific major metro areas is a concrete local-severity marker useful for regional insurance/reinsurance climate-risk repricing and municipal infrastructure-stress assessments.
insights.quote: Salt Lake City hit 109 degrees Fahrenheit on July 12
insights.locator: Many of the busted records date back

insights.claim: Even Southern California, an area that typically escapes countrywide heat waves, endured excessive heat warnings during the second week of September 2026.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: Heat reaching historically heat-insulated coastal California signals broader geographic spread of extreme-heat exposure, relevant for regional real estate, agriculture, and wildfire-risk underwriting.
insights.quote: Much of Southern California endured excessive heat warnings during the second week of September as hot conditions and soupy air made Rodeo Drive feel more like Bourbon Street.

insights.claim: Climate change is described as the primary driver of the extreme US heat because it raises the baseline average temperature, making already-hot days hit more extreme peaks than the same weather pattern would have produced decades ago.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: Frames climate change as a persistent baseline shift rather than a one-off event — implies structurally higher average cooling demand and heat-related risk going forward, not just a single anomalous season.
insights.quote: Climate change is far and away the primary driver of the extreme heat baking the US.
insights.locator: Why Has Fall Started So Hot?

insights.claim: Rising overnight temperatures are a particularly dangerous element of the current heat pattern because the lack of nighttime cooling prevents the body from recovering from daytime heat stress, making heat waves more deadly even when daytime highs aren't record-setting.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: Overnight-low trends, not just daytime highs, are the metric to watch for public-health and mortality risk from heat — relevant to health-system capacity planning and heat-related insurance claims modeling.
insights.quote: The lack of relief is what makes heat waves particularly deadly; without beneficial overnight cooling, heat stress becomes too much for many people to withstand.
insights.locator: That trend has been especially notable at night

insights.claim: A warmer climate is altering upper-atmosphere patterns to favor 'heat domes' — strong high-pressure centers aloft that force air to sink and compress, heating it further, which combines with strong sunshine and dry soils to push temperatures well above normal, and these ridges are becoming more common in a warming world.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: A clear causal chain (warming → more frequent heat domes → more extreme surface heat) that can be used as a forward-looking model for predicting when/where extreme-heat events recur, useful for ag-commodity and energy-demand forecasting.
insights.quote: Strong centers of high pressure aloft force air to sink toward the ground. This air heats up as it compresses, combining with intense sunshine and dry soils to ratchet the heat well above normal.
insights.locator: A warmer climate is also altering

themes.theme: El Niño as a forward-looking indicator

insights.claim: The current El Niño event — a pattern of warmer-than-normal Pacific Ocean waters that alters the jet stream and global weather — is shaping up to be a record-setting event in 2026.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: A record-strength El Niño is a known, trackable macro forcing pattern with historically consistent seasonal effects, making it a usable input for winter energy-demand and agricultural-yield forecasting models.
insights.quote: This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be a record-setting event.

insights.claim: El Niño's strongest effects on US weather are typically felt during the cold months, since the abnormally warm Pacific waters alter the jet stream that governs autumn and winter weather patterns.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: Implies the current heat is a leading indicator rather than the peak effect — the bigger El Niño-driven weather impact is still to come this winter, which is the window that matters most for heating-demand and winter-crop forecasts.
insights.quote: We typically feel El Niño’s greatest effects during the cold months
insights.locator: We typically feel El Niño’s greatest effects

insights.claim: Based on the patterns of previous strong El Niño events, forecasters expect a vast swath of the US to run warmer than normal through fall and winter 2026, meaning additional heat records are likely to keep falling this year.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: A specific, dated forecast (warm fall/winter, more records to break) that can be tracked against actual outcomes over the next two quarters as a check on forecaster credibility and a live input to seasonal energy/ag positioning.
insights.quote: we’re likely not done breaking heat records yet this year
insights.locator: This year’s El Niño is shaping up

insights.claim: Computer models as of mid-September 2026 show a pronounced atmospheric ridge pattern likely to lock in widespread unseasonable warmth across the US through at least the end of September, with the Upper Midwest and Deep South facing the greatest odds of above-normal temperatures and some models showing 5-10°F above-normal readings for the back half of the month.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: Gives specific regions (Upper Midwest, Deep South) and a magnitude (5-10°F) for near-term heat exposure, directly usable for short-horizon regional energy-demand and crop-stress positioning.
insights.quote: temperatures could run 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above normal for the latter half of September
insights.locator: Computer models show a pronounced ridge pattern
